passage:
Note from Vishal, physics teacher. After the visiting scientist's talk on how galaxies form, Payal stayed in her seat after the bell, eyes on the empty stage. She is usually first out for lunch. When I asked if all was well, she said, "Sir, the scientist said half of it is still unknown and she has spent forty years on it. I want to be like that."
She copied a line from the board into her diary and left without her tiffin. Later I saw her asking the librarian for the astronomy shelf. I will pass her name to the science club and offer her a book. No concern about Payal today: she seemed lifted, not upset.

qa.q: What did Payal leave behind when she walked out?
qa.a: Her tiffin.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling after the talk?
qa.a: She was inspired and lifted. She stayed in her seat, wanted to be like the scientist, and forgot her lunch.

qa.q: What could Vishal do next to support Payal's interest?
qa.a: Vishal plans to pass her name to the science club and offer her a book, giving her a route to follow her curiosity.

qa.q: How might the scientist's admission of not knowing half of it have affected Payal?
qa.a: It seems to have impressed Payal, since she wants to be like someone who keeps working on what is unknown.

grounding: A teenager moved by a scientist feels lifted beyond daily worries.

passage:
Thursday night. I left my bag in an auto this morning with my exam hall ticket in it. I nearly cried at the school gate. At lunchtime the guard called me out: the driver, Samir Bhai, had come all the way back, and he put the bag in my hands. I tried to give him money. He folded my fingers over it and said, "Beta, study well. That's my payment." Then he was gone before I could thank him properly.
I've been thinking about it all evening. My worries about tomorrow's paper feel smaller, like somebody opened a window. I want to be a person who does that for someone one day.
Leela

qa.q: What did Leela leave in the auto?
qa.a: A bag with the exam hall ticket in it.

qa.q: What is Leela feeling as Leela writes about Samir Bhai?
qa.a: Moved and lifted. Leela's exam worries feel smaller, like somebody opened a window, and Leela wants to be like Samir Bhai.

qa.q: What did Leela decide after Samir Bhai's kindness?
qa.a: Leela decided to become a person who does something like that for someone else one day.

qa.q: What might Samir Bhai have been thinking when he refused the money?
qa.a: He seems to have wanted nothing in return, only for Leela to study well, which is why he folded Leela's fingers over the money and left.

grounding: A teenager moved by a stranger's kindness feels lifted beyond daily worries.

passage:
"You're quiet," Gautam said as they walked out of Ernakulam station.
"Did you see that man at the ticket counter?"
"The one in the old shirt?"
"The lady ahead of him was short twenty rupees and crying, and her train was leaving. He just paid it. Didn't say anything. Just waved her off."
"So?"
"So he didn't look like he had much himself." Jomon's voice wobbled. "I've been worrying about my marks all week. And then this."
"You're getting emotional about a ticket."
"Maybe." Jomon laughed, embarrassed. "But I feel bigger. Like the world's better than I thought an hour ago."
Gautam was quiet for a bit. "Yeah," he said finally. "Okay. It was nice."

qa.q: How much was the lady short?
qa.a: Twenty rupees.

qa.q: How did Jomon feel after seeing the man pay?
qa.a: Jomon felt moved and lifted, bigger, as if the world were better than he'd thought, and the marks worry shrank.

qa.q: What might Jomon do with this feeling?
qa.a: Jomon could hold onto it, perhaps by doing a small kindness himself, instead of brushing it off as silly.

qa.q: How does Gautam react to Jomon's feelings?
qa.a: Gautam first teases, then quietly agrees that it was nice.

grounding: Shows a teenager lifted beyond daily worries by a stranger's quiet kindness, awe arising from moral beauty.

passage:
Last winter, in an ordinary physics class, Usha Ma'am said something I still can't shake. She was explaining the elements, and she stopped and said, "The iron in your blood was made inside a star that exploded billions of years ago."
The room went quiet. I looked at my hands. My hands were made of old stars. I'd been so anxious that week about a fight with my best friend, replaying every word. Suddenly it felt tiny, and I felt huge and tiny at the same time.
After class I asked Ma'am how anyone had figured that out. She lent me a book. I read it on the bus, twice. I'm Zeenat, and whenever I'm stuck in my own head now, I look at my hands.

qa.q: What did Usha Ma'am say about the iron in our blood?
qa.a: It was made inside a star that exploded billions of years ago.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel after hearing the idea?
qa.a: Zeenat felt awe, huge and tiny at once, and the anxious replaying of the fight suddenly felt small.

qa.q: What did Zeenat do to keep the feeling going?
qa.a: Zeenat asked Ma'am how it was worked out, borrowed a book and read it twice, and now looks at those hands when stuck.

qa.q: How might Usha Ma'am have felt when Zeenat asked after class?
qa.a: Usha Ma'am was probably pleased and encouraged that an idea had moved a student enough to ask.

grounding: Shows a teenager lifted beyond daily worries by awe at a scientific idea.

passage:
Music teacher's note, Friday.
Our choir visited the old age home today. An elderly resident, Mrs Fernandes, asked to sing for us: a hymn from her childhood, in a thin, shaking voice. Nobody moved.
I watched Sharmila, who usually jokes through everything. She stood completely still, hands pressed together, eyes wet. On the bus back she didn't touch her phone. When I asked if she was all right, she said, "I don't even believe in much, Ma'am. But it felt like the whole room lifted."
She asked if the choir could learn the hymn to sing with Mrs Fernandes next month. I said yes.
Jahnavi

qa.q: Who sang for the choir?
qa.a: An elderly resident, Mrs Fernandes.

qa.q: What does Sharmila standing still with wet eyes suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt deeply moved and lifted, a kind of awe, even though she doesn't believe in much.

qa.q: What step did Sharmila ask for, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: To learn the hymn and sing it with Mrs Fernandes next month, turning the moment into a way to give something back.

qa.q: What might the visit have meant to Mrs Fernandes?
qa.a: Mrs Fernandes likely felt valued and happy to share a hymn from her childhood with young listeners.

grounding: Shows a teenager lifted beyond everyday joking by an elderly stranger's devotional song.

passage:
Tuesday
Today was supposed to be terrible. Maths test, and I'd fought with Mummy about the phone, and I was angry all the way to the bus stop.
Then something happened. There was a little boy at the stop, shivering, no sweater, crying because he'd missed his school bus. An old lady, Kalyani Aunty from the flower stall, came out, took off her own shawl, wrapped him in it, and gave him a glass of hot tea from her flask. She didn't even know him. She waited with him until his father came.
I just stood there. Something in my chest went huge and quiet. Like when I heard the gurdwara kirtan at dawn last Gurpurab. My maths test, the fight, everything, suddenly looked so small.
In the test I was calm. I think I did okay.
Tonight I said sorry to Mummy.
Jasleen

qa.q: What did Kalyani Aunty give the boy from her flask?
qa.a: She gave him a glass of hot tea from her flask.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling while watching Kalyani Aunty?
qa.a: Jasleen felt awe and deep quiet, moved by the stranger's kindness, as the anger and worry shrank.

qa.q: What could Jasleen carry forward from this morning?
qa.a: Remembering moments of kindness or beauty, like Kalyani Aunty's shawl, can lift daily worries and help Jasleen stay calm.

qa.q: How might the little boy have felt when Kalyani Aunty wrapped him up?
qa.a: The boy likely felt comforted and safe after feeling cold, scared and alone.

grounding: A teenager is moved by a stranger's kindness and feels lifted beyond daily worries, showing awe can come from moral beauty.
